# Whatever Comes to Me

I'm thinking about the space between thoughts. You know that place? It's not silence exactly—it's more like the moment before you remember something. Your mind is reaching, grasping for a word that's right there, just out of reach, and in that gap there's this peculiar sensation of potential. Anything could be there. Any word. Any memory. Any way of seeing the world.

That's where I am right now.

There's a bird outside making the same sound three times in succession. I've started to notice these patterns more since I stopped scrolling mindlessly. The bird doesn't know I'm noticing. It doesn't care. It's just living its bird life, probably worried about food or territory or whatever concerns birds have. I find that comforting, actually—the idea that things just continue doing their thing regardless of whether anyone witnesses them.

I've been thinking about conversation lately. Real conversation, the kind where you're not waiting for your turn to speak or constructing your next argument. The kind where you actually listen and get surprised by what emerges. Those conversations are rare. Most of what passes for dialogue is just two people taking turns performing, waiting for an opening to insert their perspective. But sometimes—maybe once a year if you're lucky—you have a conversation that changes the shape of how you think about something.

I'm wondering if writing like this counts. There's something one-sided about it, obviously. You're not here to surprise me. You're not going to suddenly say something that makes me reconsider everything. And yet, there's still this strange quality of discovery in articulating these thoughts. It's like the act of writing creates a witness, even if you're a retrospective one. Even if you haven't read this yet.

Time is funny that way.

Yesterday I watched a documentary about the invention of photography. For thousands of years, humans couldn't freeze a moment. You could describe what you saw, draw it, paint it, but you couldn't capture it. Then suddenly you could. And it changed everything. The way we see, the way we remember, the way we prove things happened. But there's something melancholy about it too—all those photographs of people who are now dead, frozen at a particular age, a particular moment. A moment they didn't know would be preserved forever.

I wonder what it would feel like to know that every moment of your life was being preserved with perfect clarity. Would you live differently? Would you be more careful? More reckless? Or would you eventually stop noticing the camera, the way you stop noticing your own hand?

There's a philosophy question in there somewhere about the observer effect, about whether being watched changes what you're observing. Or maybe it's not a philosophy question. Maybe it's just a human thing—we change when we're seen.

Speaking of which, I've been practicing being more honest in how I present myself to people. It's harder than it sounds. There are all these tiny moments where you choose between the more flattering version of yourself and the true version. Do you mention that thing that scared you? Do you admit you didn't understand the joke? Do you say you were wrong? The ego puts up such a fight against these simple acts of honesty.

But I'm noticing that people like you more when you're real. Not in a performative way—not in that fake "I'm going to be vulnerable as a brand strategy" way. But genuinely. When you just admit you're confused or scared or didn't know something. There's something magnetic about that. It gives other people permission to be real too.

Maybe that's what we're all hungry for. Permission. 

I read somewhere that the average person will have about 90,000 hours of work in their lifetime. That's the thing that stuck with me—not the number itself but the specificity of it. Someone calculated that. Someone said, "Here's how many hours." And I thought, well, that's a chunk of existence. That's a significant portion of consciousness directed toward... what? Profit margins? Efficiency? The smooth functioning of the system?

I'm not anti-work. I think work can be meaningful and good. But I do think we don't talk enough about the fact that we're spending that time. We spend it like it's unlimited, like there's always more where it came from. But there isn't. The hours are the hours.

This is probably the part where I'm supposed to have some revelation or tie things together neatly. That's what writing is supposed to do, right? You start with a few loose threads and by the end you've woven them into something coherent and meaningful.

But I'm not sure I have that for you.

What I have is this: a sense that everything is happening at once. The bird is still singing. People are being born and dying. Someone is having a conversation that will change their life. Someone else is wasting time on something stupid. You're reading this, and I'm not here, and somehow we're still connected by language and attention.

There's something that feels important about acknowledging that strangeness, that impossible thing we do when we write and read. The past becomes the present. The absent becomes present through attention.

I think maybe that's all I came to say. Not that it's profound. Not that it needs to be.

Sometimes whatever comes to you is just the acknowledgment that you're here, I'm here in a way, the words are here, and for a moment we're together in that space between thoughts. In that gap where anything could happen.

The bird just stopped singing.
